claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
Dislocation accumulation at internal boundaries contributes to the starting alloy's limited ductility and brittleness.
A controlled sub-critical thermal aging treatment will produce nanoscale precipitates in the alloy.
The aging-induced precipitates will form preferentially along internal lamellar or colony boundaries.
The aging-induced precipitates will be coherent with the surrounding microstructure.
The aging-induced precipitates will constitute a ductile phase.
Boundary precipitates will interrupt or prevent dislocation pile-ups.
The precipitates will absorb and redistribute dislocation motion as local strain dissipaters.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups will alleviate high local stress concentrations at internal boundaries.
Alleviating local stress concentrations will suppress microcracking and catastrophic damage during tensile straining.
The coherent nanoscale precipitates will strengthen the alloy through precipitation hardening.
The aging treatment will significantly increase room-temperature tensile elongation relative to the untreated alloy.
The aged alloy will retain or increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Precipitate coarsening or an inhomogeneous precipitate distribution could compromise mechanical performance.
The untreated alloy exhibits dislocation pile-ups, local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic brittle failure under room-temperature tensile loading.
